source.title: Life after BERT: What do Other Muppets Understand about Language?
source.authors: Vladislav Lialin; Kevin Zhao; Namrata Shivagunde; Anna Rumshisky

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether downstream task performance is associated with parameter count, using benchmark accuracy and rank correlations rather than held-out loss or fitted scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study measures zero-shot linguistic benchmark accuracy, not held-out cross-entropy loss, compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocations. Scaling-law results mentioned from other work are citations, not this study's results. The relevant reported test is the relationship between parameter count and downstream task accuracy.
record.test_reason: The study's own zero-shot results relate parameter count within GPT2, ALBERT and T5 families to downstream oLMpics accuracy, using Spearman rank correlation. It tests V6 by a different method. No loss, compute or fitted-law results are reported, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that parameter count within a model family does not correlate with zero-shot performance on oLMpics and psycholinguistic tasks, contrary to expectations drawn from scaling-law work. They note T5 as a significant exception (except Always-Never, with Taxonomy Conjunction negative) and treat the correlation tests as anecdotal given n ≤ 4.
record.recipe_differences: Uses zero-shot linguistic probing and benchmark accuracy rather than held-out loss sweeps, power-law fits, or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and model family affect the reported size-performance relationship. Prompt wording also changes Antonym Negation accuracy, and the effects vary across GPT2 sizes.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2022
record.problems: The study itself notes that the sample size for each size-correlation test is ≤ 4 and calls those results anecdotal. It measures downstream task accuracy rather than held-out loss.
record.rows_left_out: Not every per-model, per-task score in Tables 3–6 is recorded; rows focus on the explicitly reported size-correlation results and the prompt condition the authors use to show a smaller GPT2 outperforming the largest.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted or quantitative trend of downstream performance with scale; models above 2.8B; tasks beyond zero-shot linguistic probes.
Not tested; no loss is measured.

missing.what: Psycholinguistic top-5 accuracy rises largely with size within T5 (CPRAG 20.6→41.1→50.0→58.8; ROLE 9.1→44.3) and ALBERTv2 (CPRAG 41.4→85.3). This supports V6 but no row records it, and it partly contradicts the authors' 'size does not correlate' summary.
GPT2 Antonym Negation under the original oLMpics prompt rises with size (53.3, 52.8, 59.0, 60.6), the contrast case for the prompt #4 reversal.
Per-model zero-shot oLMpics accuracies by family (e.g. GPT2 Age Comparison 47.6, 50.1, 69.6, 51.9, non-monotone), underlying the correlation tests.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence on V6 is weak: few models per family, near-random accuracy on several tasks (where no scaling can show), and a doubtful p-value for T5. The authors' blanket conclusion understates the size trends visible in Table 5 for T5 and ALBERT. Kaplan et al. is only cited as received wisdom; no loss-law result is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of loss laws fitted on small runs to larger runs.
Architecture effects on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability from pretraining loss; downstream tasks beyond the tested linguistic benchmarks and model families.
Dependence of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup, and departures of loss curves from power laws.

rows.subject: GPT2 models
rows.size_stated: different versions; 14M–2.8B parameters across the evaluated model families; GPT2 sizes are also listed in Table 4
rows.operation_detail: Spearman correlation of model size with oLMpics task accuracy

conditions.value: all GPT2 tests reported in Section 4.2

rows.measure: Spearman rank correlation between model accuracy and model size
rows.value: No rank-correlation; p-value > 0.05 for all GPT2 tests
rows.note: The authors caution that the sample size for each test is ≤ 4, so they describe these results as anecdotal.
rows.check: The extracted text drops the comparison symbol ("p-value  0.05"); the record's reading of >0.05 fits the authors' interpretation. Each test has n ≤ 4 models, which the authors call anecdotal. Table 4 shows GPT2large beating GPT2xl on Age Comparison (69.6 vs 51.9).

rows.subject: ALBERT models (v1 and v2)
rows.size_stated: 12M–235M trainable parameters for ALBERT; individual evaluated sizes are listed in Table 4
rows.operation_detail: Spearman correlation of model size with oLMpics task accuracy

conditions.value: all ALBERT v1 and v2 tests reported in Section 4.2

rows.measure: Spearman rank correlation between model accuracy and model size
rows.value: No rank-correlation; p-value > 0.05 for all ALBERT v1 and v2 tests
rows.note: The authors caution that the sample size for each test is ≤ 4, so they describe these results as anecdotal.
rows.check: Same missing comparison symbol and n ≤ 4 caveat as r1.

rows.subject: T5 models
rows.size_stated: 233M–2.8B parameters; the study evaluates T5 sizes listed in Table 4
rows.operation_detail: Spearman correlation of model size with oLMpics task accuracy

conditions.value: T5 oLMpics tasks except Always-Never and Taxonomy Conjunction

rows.measure: Spearman rank correlation between model accuracy and model size
rows.uncertainty: p-value approximately 10^-6; multiple-hypothesis testing adjusted using Bonferroni's method
rows.note: The paper states the strong correlation applies to all T5 tasks except Always-Never, then separately reports a negative correlation for Taxonomy Conjunction.
rows.check: The reported p ~10^-6 for a Spearman correlation on at most 4 models is implausible, perhaps pooled or mis-stated. The text also says 'all tasks except Always-Never' yet reports a negative Taxonomy Conjunction correlation, so the scope of the T5 claim is internally inconsistent.

rows.subject: T5 models
rows.size_stated: 233M–2.8B parameters; the study evaluates T5 sizes listed in Table 4
rows.operation_detail: Spearman correlation of model size with oLMpics task accuracy
rows.measure: Direction of Spearman correlation between model accuracy and model size
rows.value: Correlation is negative; coefficient and p-value not stated
rows.note: The reported negative direction is contrary to downstream performance improving with size.
rows.check: No coefficient or p-value is given. T5 Taxonomy Conjunction values in Table 4 cannot be cleanly aligned in the extracted text.

rows.subject: GPT2base
rows.note: The authors report that prompt #4 lets the smallest model outperform the largest by approximately 10%.
rows.check: A single model's accuracy is not a scaling result on its own. It is the comparison point for r6 and should be merged into r6 rather than marked observed.

rows.subject: GPT2xl
rows.note: The smaller GPT2base scores 59.6 under the same prompt; the text characterizes the difference as approximately 10%.
rows.check: Under prompt #4 GPT2xl scores 48.4 vs GPT2base 59.6, below the 50% random baseline. Under the original oLMpics prompt (53.3→52.8→59.0→60.6) and prompt #1, accuracy roughly rises with size, so the reversal depends on the prompt.

relationships.condition: GPT2 (0.1B–1.5B) and ALBERT v1/v2 families, zero-shot oLMpics
relationships.reason: No significant size–accuracy rank correlation in any test (r1, r2); evidence is weak because each test has n ≤ 4.
relationships.display_finding: No test showed a significant size–accuracy rank correlation for GPT2 or ALBERT, although each comparison contained at most 4 models.

relationships.condition: T5 family (small to xl), zero-shot oLMpics tasks other than Always-Never and Taxonomy Conjunction
relationships.reason: Reported Spearman correlation is 1.0 and significant (r3), though the significance claim is doubtful with n ≤ 4.
relationships.display_finding: The reported Spearman correlation was 1.0, although the claimed statistical significance is uncertain with at most four models.

relationships.reason: Correlation of size with accuracy is reported as negative (r4).
relationships.display_finding: T5 accuracy was negatively correlated with model size.

relationships.condition: GPT2 Antonym Negation across prompt wordings
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with size under the original prompt but reverses under prompt #4 (base 59.6 vs xl 48.4), so the scaling trend depends on the prompt (r6).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increases with size under the original prompt but falls from 59.6 for base to 48.4 for xl under prompt 4.
